description: We are we 1 win, a team participating in the Sibu NASA Space Apps Challenge. We aim to bring the stories of NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars to life through design, animation and interactive storytelling.
summary: Still Here: Flight 73 turns NASA’s retired Mars hardware into an interactive story for school-age space explorers. Ingenuity, grounded after its 72nd flight, imagines one more journey to the landers and rovers whose work on Mars is done. Visitors travel across a NASA-textured Mars globe, explore nine sites, hear each machine’s story, and try a hands-on science or engineering interaction at every stop. Real mission sources, Mars solar time, Sun direction and great-circle distances anchor the experience; the imagined flight is clearly labelled fiction. A flight log, downloadable postcard and life-size AR Hangar bring the machines’ continuing scientific legacy closer to learners.
details:
THE IDEA AND THE CHALLENGE

Ingenuity flew 72 times on Mars. Flight 73 is the journey it never got to make. Our interactive 3D story uses this grounded aircraft as a guide to NASA hardware whose missions on Mars have ended, showing what each machine discovered and what later missions inherited. The imagined flight and first-person machine voices are storytelling devices, clearly distinguished from sourced mission facts.

HOW THE EXPERIENCE WORKS

The visitor first attempts a rotor test: the real, damaged Ingenuity stays on the ground while an imagined companion lifts off. The route visits Viking 1, Viking 2, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Perseverance’s discarded backshell and parachute, and Ingenuity’s home. At each stop, visitors can orbit the hardware, open story hotspots and try a hands-on interaction: scan an early surface photograph, move a rover down a ramp, explore a stuck wheel or dust storm, reveal a marsquake, or decode a parachute message.

The globe uses NASA Viking imagery and MOLA relief. Travel headings and distances use great-circle calculations; Mars solar time and Sun direction use the published Mars24 method. Radio calls use computed Earth–Mars light time, with the experience’s time compression identified. Visitors can change the time of sol to explore the lighting. The flight log ends with a locally downloadable postcard, and the AR Hangar lets compatible Android WebXR devices place the machines at life size.

EDUCATIONAL VALUE AND ORIGINALITY

The experience is designed for school-age space enthusiasts and other curious visitors. Its central idea is a line of inheritance: a mission can stop operating while its discoveries, engineering lessons and scientific data keep helping later missions. Combining an abandoned machine’s imagined journey, chronological encounters, sourced facts and hands-on actions makes this legacy something visitors explore rather than only read.

IMPLEMENTATION AND ACCURACY

Built with React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, drei, Zustand and Vite, the project runs as a static, client-side website without accounts or analytics. The main story is intended for a desktop WebGL 2 browser; phone AR depends on device and browser support. NASA source models are credited, while authored or adapted Blender reconstructions, surface treatments and interactive effects are identified as illustrative. They are not measured present-day resting conditions. Dates, coordinates, numerical claims and approximation notes are documented with per-claim links in docs/FACT_CHECK.md. The fictional route is far beyond Ingenuity’s real flight capability.

AI / SI DISCLOSURE

The team directed the concept, challenge choice, audience and review. Claude Code assisted most code and drafted narration and machine stories. OpenAI Codex assisted Blender Python reconstruction and model processing. These are AI-assisted code and text, with illustrative procedural 3D reconstructions. Spoken narration is AI-generated locally using Kokoro-82M; Ingenuity’s radio treatment is custom Python processing, and other sounds are synthesized in the browser. The demo records the working project and uses AI-generated speech. Detailed attribution, source-model distinctions and software licences are published in AI_USAGE.md and CREDITS.md. NASA does not endorse this independent project.
